# Module `websocket`

websocket - an RFC 6455 WebSocket CLIENT over TCP sockets.

The client half of the protocol: the opening handshake, masked frame
emission, and frame parsing for text / binary / ping / pong / close. The
server half (accepting an upgrade on an inbound connection) is deliberately
NOT here — a WebSocket server needs the HTTP surface's request parsing and a
per-connection lifetime policy, which belong to `http`; this module stays the
client a program uses to talk to somebody else's WS endpoint.

Why this exists: every JSON-RPC control plane worth talking to (Hermes'
dashboard `/api/ws` among them) speaks WebSocket and nothing else. Without a
client, a Vyb program cannot drive those services at all, no matter how good
its HTTP story is.

Usage (connect and exchange one text message):
  import websocket::{ws_connect, ws_send_text, ws_recv_text, ws_close, WsConn}
  conn<WsConn> = ws_connect("127.0.0.1", 9119, "/api/ws?token=...", 15000) else WsConn { ... }
  ws_send_text(conn.ws, "hello")
  reply<String> = ws_recv_text(conn.ws, conn.pending) else ""

`ws_connect` is the one-call path. It blocks on the response, so a program
that must answer the peer inside the same thread should use the split form:
`ws_send_handshake(fd, ...)` then `ws_finish_handshake(fd, ...)`.

Handshake: RFC 6455 §4.1 — GET with `Upgrade: websocket`, a 16-byte base64
`Sec-WebSocket-Key`, and `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`. The response must be
`101 Switching Protocols` carrying `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, which is
base64(SHA1(key + "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11")). Both halves cross
the runtime: `vyb_ws_accept_key` computes the expected accept value and
`vyb_base64_encode` encodes the nonce, so the stdlib neither ships SHA-1 as a
general primitive nor re-implements base64 in Vyb.

Framing: RFC 6455 §5. Clients MUST mask every frame (§5.3); the mask key is
4 random bytes (`rand`), and the payload is XORed with it positionally. We
mask unconditionally — a masked client frame is always legal, an unmasked one
is a protocol-error close. Reserved bits are never set, so no extensions are
negotiated.

Fallibility: every transport operation is `T?` — absence IS the failed
operation. `ws_connect` / `ws_finish_handshake` return `WsConn?`, `ws_send_text`
/ `ws_send_binary` / `ws_ping` / `ws_close` return `Bool?`, `ws_recv_frame` /
`ws_recv_text` return `WsRead?` / `String?`, with `ws_error_code()` /
`ws_error_message()` naming why. No `-1`/`""` sentinel is ever smuggled out as
data.

<a id="sym-ws_connect"></a>
### `ws_connect` · fn

```
ws_connect(host<String>, port<Int>, path<String>, timeout_ms<Int>)<WsConn?> ->
```

Open a TCP connection to `host`:`port`, perform the RFC 6455 client
handshake for `path` (include the query string, e.g. "/api/ws?token=..."),
and return the live socket with any bytes that arrived after the head.

Absent on: connect failure, a non-101 response, or a mismatched accept value
— `ws_error_message()` then names which. `timeout_ms` (default 15000 when 0)
bounds every subsequent read so a silent peer cannot hang the caller.

<a id="sym-ws_recv_frame"></a>
### `ws_recv_frame` · fn

```
ws_recv_frame(ws<WsSocket>, pending<String>)<WsRead?> ->
```

Receive the next DATA frame, absorbing control frames: a ping is answered
with a pong, a pong is dropped, and a close ends the stream (absent). Returns
`WsFrame?` — the data frame, or absent on close / transport failure.

Continuation frames are NOT reassembled here: each fragment is returned with
`fin` set, so a caller that sends fragmented messages can drive assembly
itself rather than inheriting a policy.

**Relationships**

- uses type [`WsRead`](#sym-wsread)
- uses type [`WsSocket`](#sym-wssocket)
